name: 2005 January GLE#69

phenomena.details: GLE#69 on January 20, 2005; the largest ground-level enhancement since February 1956 (GLE#5), with neutron monitor increases exceeding 4800% at South Pole station.
X7.1 flare on January 20, 2005 from AR 10720.
Strong SEP event; >10 MeV proton flux peaked near 1860 pfu (S3). Its distinction was a hard, relativistic spectrum that produced the largest GLE since 1956 rather than an extreme >10 MeV fluence.
Severe radio blackout from the X7.1 flare.

impacts.description: Extreme radiation dose rates at aviation altitudes; the FAA issued a rare space weather advisory. Airline crews on polar routes would have received significant radiation exposure without rerouting. Transpolar flights were widely diverted.
Severe HF radio blackout across the sunlit hemisphere from the X7.1 flare; polar cap absorption persisted for days due to the intense SEP event.

Multiple spacecraft experienced elevated single-event upset rates; some sensors were temporarily blinded by the intense particle flux. The Mars rovers Spirit and Opportunity also detected elevated radiation.

papers.title: GIANT GROUND LEVEL ENHANCEMENT OF RELATIVISTIC SOLAR PROTONS ON 2005 JANUARY 20. I. SPACESHIP EARTH OBSERVATIONS
papers.authors: Bieber, J. W., Clem, J., Evenson, P., et al.
papers.keyFinding: Spaceship Earth neutron-monitor analysis of the giant 20 January 2005 ground-level enhancement, the largest since 1956.

summary: GLE#69 on January 20, 2005 was the largest ground-level enhancement since 1956 (GLE#5), driven by an X7.1 flare from AR 10720. The South Pole neutron monitor recorded increases exceeding 4800%, prompting extreme aviation radiation alerts and widespread flight diversions from polar routes.
description: On January 20, 2005, an X7.1 flare from AR 10720 produced GLE#69 – the largest ground-level enhancement since February 1956. The South Pole neutron monitor recorded a count rate increase exceeding 4800%, indicating an extraordinarily hard and intense relativistic proton spectrum. The FAA issued a rare space weather advisory, and airlines worldwide diverted polar route flights to lower latitudes to reduce crew and passenger radiation exposure. The associated SEP event reached S3 (strong) levels by >10 MeV proton flux (peaking near 1860 pfu), but its exceptionally hard, relativistic spectrum produced the largest GLE since 1956. Despite the extreme radiation storm, the geomagnetic storm was relatively moderate (Dst ~ −105 nT), illustrating that radiation storms and geomagnetic storms can be decoupled. The event remains one of the benchmark events for aviation radiation exposure planning.
